iitjam-2024-01.title: Solve the Bernoulli equation
iitjam-2024-01.body:
Put $v=y^{-2}$. Then $v'=-2y^{-3}y'=-2y^{-3}(y-y^3)=-2v+2$, a linear equation with solution
$$v(x)=1+\left(\frac1{c^2}-1\right)e^{-2x}.$$
So $y_c(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+(c^{-2}-1)e^{-2x}}}$, which is positive and defined for all $x\ge0$, and $y_c(x)\to1$ as $x\to\infty$.

**Answer: (B)**

iitjam-2024-01.title: Phase line
iitjam-2024-01.body:
The equation is autonomous: $y'=y-y^3=y(1-y)(1+y)$. For $y>0$ the only equilibrium is $y=1$. If $0<y<1$ then $y'>0$; if $y>1$ then $y'<0$. So a solution starting at any $c>0$ moves monotonically toward $1$ and cannot cross it; a bounded monotone solution converges to an equilibrium, so the limit is $1$.

**Answer: (B)**

iitjam-2024-02.title: Use the wave equation
iitjam-2024-02.body:
Let $G$ be an antiderivative of $g$ and $w=y\,u_g=G(x+y)-G(x-y)$. Then
$w_{xx}=g'(x+y)-g'(x-y)=w_{yy}$.

Now $w_{xx}=y\,u_{xx}$, while $w_y=u+y\,u_y$ and $w_{yy}=2u_y+y\,u_{yy}$. Hence
$$y\,u_{xx}=2u_y+y\,u_{yy}\iff u_{xx}=\frac2y\,u_y+u_{yy}.$$

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-03.title: Integrating factor
iitjam-2024-03.body:
Write $y'-y\sec x=1$. An integrating factor is $e^{-\int\sec x\,dx}=\dfrac{1}{\sec x+\tan x}=\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}$. Then
$$\left(\frac{y\cos x}{1+\sin x}\right)'=\frac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}\implies \frac{y\cos x}{1+\sin x}=\log(1+\sin x)+C.$$
$y(0)=0$ gives $C=0$, so $y=(\sec x+\tan x)\log(1+\sin x)$.

At $x=\pi/6$: $\sec x+\tan x=\frac2{\sqrt3}+\frac1{\sqrt3}=\sqrt3$ and $1+\sin x=\frac32$. So $y(\pi/6)=\sqrt3\log\frac32$.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-03.title: Verify the candidate
iitjam-2024-03.body:
Check $y=(\sec x+\tan x)\log(1+\sin x)$ directly: $(\sec x+\tan x)'=\sec x(\sec x+\tan x)$, and $(\sec x+\tan x)\cdot\frac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}=1$. So
$y'=\sec x\cdot y+1$ ✓ and $y(0)=0$ ✓. By uniqueness this is the solution, and $y(\pi/6)=\sqrt3\log(3/2)$.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-04.title: Eliminate the parameter
iitjam-2024-04.body:
Differentiate: $2x+2h(y+xy')+2yy'=0$, so $y'=-\dfrac{x+hy}{hx+y}$. From the curve, $h=\dfrac{1-x^2-y^2}{2xy}$, so
$$x+hy=\frac{x^2-y^2+1}{2x},\qquad hx+y=\frac{1-x^2+y^2}{2y}.$$
Hence the family satisfies $y'=-\dfrac{y(x^2-y^2+1)}{x(1-x^2+y^2)}$.

Orthogonal trajectories have slope $-1/y'$:
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x(1-x^2+y^2)}{y(x^2-y^2+1)}\iff (x^2y-y^3+y)\frac{dy}{dx}-(xy^2-x^3+x)=0.$$

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-04.title: Check at a point
iitjam-2024-04.body:
The point $(x,y)=(1,\frac12)$ lies on the member with $h=\frac{1-x^2-y^2}{2xy}=-\frac14$. The family's slope there is $-\frac{x+hy}{hx+y}=-\frac{1-1/8}{-1/4+1/2}=-\frac72$, so the orthogonal slope is $\frac27$.

In (A): $x^2y-y^3+y=\frac12-\frac18+\frac12=\frac78$ and $xy^2-x^3+x=\frac14$, giving $y'=\frac{1/4}{7/8}=\frac27$ ✓. (B) gives $-\frac27$; in (C), (D) the coefficients are $\frac98$ and $\frac94$, giving $y'=\pm2$.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-05.title: Internal direct product
iitjam-2024-05.body:
The unique subgroups $H$ (order 3) and $K$ (order 13) are normal (conjugates of a subgroup have the same order). $H\cap K=\{e\}$ and $|HK|=39$, so $G\cong H\times K\cong\mathbb Z_3\times\mathbb Z_{13}\cong\mathbb Z_{39}$, which is cyclic.

(D) is false: the unique subgroup of order 13 contains exactly 12 elements of order 13.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-05.title: Count elements
iitjam-2024-05.body:
Every element has order 1, 3, 13 or 39. Elements of order 3 lie in the unique subgroup of order 3 (2 of them), elements of order 13 lie in the unique subgroup of order 13 (12 of them). With the identity that is $15<39$ elements, so some element has order 39 and $G$ is cyclic.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-06.title: Look at element orders
iitjam-2024-06.body:
All four groups have order 4.

- $U(5)=\{1,2,3,4\}$: $2$ has order 4, so $U(5)\cong\mathbb Z_4$.
- $U(10)=\{1,3,7,9\}$: $3$ has order 4 ($3^2=9$), so $U(10)\cong\mathbb Z_4$.
- $U(8)=\{1,3,5,7\}$: every square is $1$, so $U(8)\cong\mathbb Z_2\times\mathbb Z_2$.
- $U(12)=\{1,5,7,11\}$: $5^2=25\equiv1$, $7^2=49\equiv1$, $11^2\equiv1$, so $U(12)\cong\mathbb Z_2\times\mathbb Z_2$.

Hence only $U(8)\cong U(12)$.

**Answer: (D)**

iitjam-2024-07.title: Cycle types
iitjam-2024-07.body:
The order of a permutation is the lcm of its cycle lengths, and the cycle lengths add up to at most 13.

- 42: cycles of lengths $2,3,7$ use $12\le13$ points, lcm $=42$. So (A) is true.
- 35: lengths $5,7$ use 12 points — exists, (B) false.
- 27: needs a cycle of length divisible by 27 (since $27=3^3$ is a prime power), impossible, (C) false.
- 60: lengths $3,4,5$ use 12 points — exists, (D) false.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-08.title: Odd order rules it out
iitjam-2024-08.body:
Let $a\ne e$ with $xax^{-1}=a^{-1}$.

- If $a=a^{-1}$, then $a$ has order 2 and $|G|$ is even.
- Otherwise $a\ne a^{-1}$. Conjugation by $x$ swaps $a$ and $a^{-1}$ (since $xa^{-1}x^{-1}=(xax^{-1})^{-1}=a$), so $x^2$ commutes with $a$ while $x$ does not. If $|G|$ were odd, $x$ would have odd order $m$, and $x=(x^2)^{(m+1)/2}$ would commute with $a$, giving $a=a^{-1}$, a contradiction.

So $|G|$ is even in all cases. Examples like $S_3$ (non-abelian, $(123)$ is conjugate to $(132)$) show (C) and (D) are false.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-09.title: Counterexamples
iitjam-2024-09.body:
- **P is false:** $A=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ ($2\times1$), $b=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$: the system $x=1,\ x=1$ has the unique solution $x=1$, but $m=2\ne1=n$.
- **Q is false:** take $u\notin W$ and $v=-u$ (also $\notin W$, otherwise $u=-v\in W$). Then $u+v=0\in W$.

**Answer: (D)**

iitjam-2024-10.title: Differentiate under the integral
iitjam-2024-10.body:
Let $I(x)=\int_0^x\sin(x-t)g(t)\,dt$. By Leibniz's rule
$I'(x)=\sin(0)g(x)+\int_0^x\cos(x-t)g(t)\,dt=\int_0^x\cos(x-t)g(t)\,dt$ and
$I''(x)=g(x)-\int_0^x\sin(x-t)g(t)\,dt=g(x)-I(x)$.

So $I''+I=g$, $I(0)=0$, $I'(0)=0$. Adding $\sin x$ (which solves the homogeneous equation with $y(0)=0,y'(0)=1$) gives $y=\sin x+I(x)$.

For (C)/(D), $J(x)=\int_0^x\cos(x-t)g(t)dt$ has $J'(0)=g(0)$, which breaks $y'(0)=1$ in general, and $J''+J=g'$, not $g$.

**Answer: (B)**

iitjam-2024-10.title: Variation of parameters
iitjam-2024-10.body:
With $y_1=\cos x$, $y_2=\sin x$ (Wronskian 1), a particular solution is
$$y_p=-\cos x\int_0^x\sin t\,g(t)dt+\sin x\int_0^x\cos t\,g(t)dt=\int_0^x\sin(x-t)g(t)dt,$$
which vanishes with its derivative at $0$. So $y=\sin x+\int_0^x\sin(x-t)g(t)dt$.

**Answer: (B)**

iitjam-2024-11.title: Cycle types
iitjam-2024-11.body:
- $S_5$ and $S_6$ contain $(12)(345)$, of order 6. So (C), (D) fail.
- $A_5$: even cycle types in $S_5$ are $1$, $(2,2)$, $(3)$, $(5)$ — no element of order 4. (B) fails.
- $A_6$: even cycle types in $S_6$ are $1,(2,2),(3),(3,3),(5),(4,2)$ with orders $1,2,3,3,5,4$. Elements of order 6 would need type $(6)$ or $(3,2)$ or $(3,2,1)$, all odd. So $A_6$ has orders exactly $1,2,3,4,5$.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-12.title: Commute with a rotation and a reflection
iitjam-2024-12.body:
$G=O(2)$ consists of rotations $R_\theta$ and reflections. Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\in Z(G)$.

- Commuting with $F=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$: $AF=\begin{pmatrix}a&-b\\c&-d\end{pmatrix}$, $FA=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-c&-d\end{pmatrix}$, so $b=c=0$.
- Commuting with $R_{\pi/2}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ then forces $a=d$.

So $A=aI$ with $a^2=1$: $A=\pm I$, and both are central.

**Answer: (B)**

iitjam-2024-13.title: Use an eigenvalue
iitjam-2024-13.body:
Suppose $\dim V\ge2$ and take linearly independent $A,B\in V$. $B$ is invertible, so consider $B^{-1}A$; over $\mathbb C$ it has an eigenvalue $\lambda$. Then $\det(A-\lambda B)=\det B\cdot\det(B^{-1}A-\lambda I)=0$, yet $A-\lambda B\in V$ is nonzero (independence) — contradiction.

So $\dim V=1$, and $V=\mathbb C I_7$ shows dimension 1 does occur.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-14.title: Comparison
iitjam-2024-14.body:
- $0<a_n<\frac{1}{9n^2}$, and $\sum\frac1{n^2}$ converges.
- $0\le b_n\le\frac{n^3+1}{3^n}\le\frac{2n^3}{3^n}$, and $\sum\frac{n^3}{3^n}$ converges by the ratio test (ratio $\to\frac13$).
**Answer: (D)**

iitjam-2024-15.title: Unit vector
iitjam-2024-15.body:
$a^Ta=\frac13+\frac12+\frac16+0=1$.

- $(I-aa^T)a=a-a(a^Ta)=0$, so $I-aa^T$ has a nonzero kernel: **P false**.
- $(I-2aa^T)^2=I-4aa^T+4a(a^Ta)a^T=I$, so $I-2aa^T$ is its own inverse (a reflection): **Q true**.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-15.title: Eigenvalues
iitjam-2024-15.body:
$aa^T$ has eigenvalues $a^Ta=1$ (eigenvector $a$) and $0$ (three times, on $a^\perp$). So $I-aa^T$ has eigenvalues $0,1,1,1$ (singular) and $I-2aa^T$ has eigenvalues $-1,1,1,1$ (invertible).

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-16.title: Rank-one choices
iitjam-2024-16.body:
**P:** $Z$ is $5\times5$. Since $B$ is $5\times4$, $\operatorname{rank}B\le4<5$, so there is a nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^5$ with $v^TB=0$. Take $Z=uv^T$ for any nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^5$: $AZB=(Au)(v^TB)=0$ and $Z\ne0$. True.

**Q:** $Y$ is $4\times6$. Since $A$ is $6\times5$, $\operatorname{rank}A\le5<6$, so there is a nonzero $w\in\mathbb R^6$ with $w^TA=0$. Take $Y=uw^T$ with nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^4$: $BYA=(Bu)(w^TA)=0$. True.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-17.title: Dimension count
iitjam-2024-17.body:
$\dim P_{11}=12$.

- $E$ lies in $W=\{p:p(3)=0\}$, the kernel of the nonzero functional $p\mapsto p(3)$, so $\dim W=11$. Twelve vectors in an 11-dimensional space are dependent.
- $F$ need not be dependent: $r_0=1$ and $r_k=1+(x-4)^k$ ($1\le k\le11$) all take the value 1 at $x=4$, and they are independent (their span contains $1$ and hence every $(x-4)^k$, i.e. all of $P_{11}$).

**Answer: (B)**

iitjam-2024-18.title: Check exactness
iitjam-2024-18.body:
$M=8xy-9y^2$, $N=2x^2-6xy$. Then $M_y=8x-18y$ and $N_x=4x-6y$: not exact.

Multiply by $x^2$: $M=8x^3y-9x^2y^2$, $N=2x^4-6x^3y$. Now $M_y=8x^3-18x^2y=N_x$: exact. So $x^2$ is an integrating factor.

Both $M$ and $N$ are homogeneous of degree 2, so the equation is homogeneous, which rules out (D).

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-19.title: Simplify the minimum
iitjam-2024-19.body:
- For $x\ge0$: $\lfloor x\rfloor\ge0$, so $x-\lfloor x\rfloor\le x$ and $f(x)=\sin(x-\lfloor x\rfloor)$.
- For $x<0$: $\lfloor x\rfloor\le-1$, so $x-\lfloor x\rfloor>x$ and $f(x)=\sin x$.

So $f$ is continuous on $[-2\pi,0)$. At $0$: $f(0)=0$, left limit $\sin0=0$, right limit $\sin0=0$ — continuous. At a positive integer $n$: left limit $\sin1\ne0=f(n)$ — discontinuous. Elsewhere in $(0,2\pi]$ it is continuous.

Positive integers in $(0,2\pi]\approx(0,6.28]$: $1,\dots,6$. So $|S|=6$.

**Answer: (D)**

iitjam-2024-20.title: Rewrite as powers of $n$
iitjam-2024-20.body:
- $b_n=n\cdot n^{1/\log n}=n\cdot e$, so $\sum\frac1{b_n}=\frac1e\sum\frac1n$ diverges.
- For $n\ge3$, $\log\log n>0$, so $a_n\ge(\log n)^{\log n}=e^{\log n\cdot\log\log n}=n^{\log\log n}$. Once $\log\log n\ge2$ (i.e. $n\ge e^{e^2}$) we get $\frac1{a_n}\le\frac1{n^2}$, so $\sum\frac1{a_n}$ converges.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-21.title: Root test
iitjam-2024-21.body:
For $p>0$: $a_n^{1/n}=p\,n^{q/n}\left(1+\frac2n\right)^{-n}\to p\,e^{-2}$. So $\sum a_n$ converges when $p<e^2$ and diverges when $p>e^2$ (whatever $q$ is). Thus (A) is true, (B) false.

For $r>0$: $b_n^{1/n}=\frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{n^n}{n!}\right)^{1/n}\left(\frac{n+2}{n}\right)^{1/(2n)}\to\frac er$ (using $(n!)^{1/n}\sim n/e$). For $r<e$ this limit exceeds 1 and the series diverges, so (C) and (D) are false.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-21.title: Ratio test for $b_n$
iitjam-2024-21.body:
$\dfrac{b_{n+1}}{b_n}=\dfrac1r\left(1+\frac1n\right)^n\sqrt{\frac{(n+3)n}{(n+1)(n+2)}}\to\dfrac er$, which is $>1$ for $0<r<e$, confirming that (C), (D) fail. For $a_n$: $\log a_n=n\log p+q\log n-n^2\log(1+2/n)=n(\log p-2)+q\log n+O(1)$, which tends to $-\infty$ fast when $p<e^2$ (so $a_n\le e^{-cn}$ eventually) and to $+\infty$ when $p>e^2$.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-22.title: $T=I+D$ with $D$ nilpotent
iitjam-2024-22.body:
Let $D=\frac{d}{dx}$. On $P_7$, $D^8=0$. So $(T-I)^8=D^8=0$: (D) is true.

In the basis $1,x,\dots,x^7$, $T$ is upper triangular with all diagonal entries 1, so its only eigenvalue is 1 and $\det T=1$: $T$ is invertible (so surjective), no power of $T$ is zero, and 2 is not an eigenvalue. (A), (B), (C) are false.

**Answer: (D)**

iitjam-2024-23.title: Solve and use L'Hôpital
iitjam-2024-23.body:
With integrating factor $e^{2x}$:
$$y_\alpha(x)=\alpha e^{-2x}+\frac{\int_0^x\frac{e^{2t}}{1+t^2}dt}{e^{2x}}.$$
The first term $\to0$. In the second, numerator and denominator $\to\infty$, and by L'Hôpital the ratio has the same limit as $\dfrac{e^{2x}/(1+x^2)}{2e^{2x}}=\dfrac{1}{2(1+x^2)}\to0$.

So $y_\alpha(x)\to0$ for every $\alpha$.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-23.title: Direct estimate
iitjam-2024-23.body:
Split $\int_0^xe^{-2(x-t)}\frac{dt}{1+t^2}$ at $t=x/2$: the part over $[0,x/2]$ is at most $\frac x2e^{-x}$, and the part over $[x/2,x]$ is at most $\frac{1}{1+x^2/4}\int_{x/2}^xe^{-2(x-t)}dt\le\frac{1}{2(1+x^2/4)}$. Both $\to0$, and $\alpha e^{-2x}\to0$.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-24.title: Examples
iitjam-2024-24.body:
**P:** $f(x)=0$ for all $x$ (continuous), $g(x)=\begin{cases}1&x=1\\0&x\ne1\end{cases}$ (discontinuous at 1). Then $g\circ f\equiv g(0)=0$ is continuous.

**Q:** $f(x)=\begin{cases}1&x\in\mathbb Q\\0&x\notin\mathbb Q\end{cases}$ and $g(x)=\begin{cases}0&x\in\mathbb Q\\1&x\notin\mathbb Q\end{cases}$. Both are discontinuous everywhere, in particular at 1. But $f$ takes only the rational values $0,1$, so $g(f(x))=0$ for all $x$: continuous.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-25.title: Substitute $t=x^2$
iitjam-2024-25.body:
$f(x)=h(x^2)$ with $h(t)=\dfrac{(t+1)^2}{t^2+t+1}$, $t\ge0$.
$$h'(t)=\frac{2(t+1)(t^2+t+1)-(t+1)^2(2t+1)}{(t^2+t+1)^2}=\frac{(t+1)(1-t)}{(t^2+t+1)^2}.$$
So $h$ increases on $[0,1]$ and decreases on $[1,\infty)$.

Hence $f$ increases on $[0,1]$, decreases on $[1,\infty)$, and by evenness decreases on $[-1,0]$ and increases on $(-\infty,-1]$. Local maxima at $x=\pm1$ (value $\frac43$), local minimum at $x=0$ (value 1).

**Answer: (D)**

iitjam-2024-25.title: Derivative in $x$
iitjam-2024-25.body:
$f'(x)=h'(x^2)\cdot2x=\dfrac{2x(x^2+1)(1-x^2)}{(x^4+x^2+1)^2}$. Sign changes: $+$ on $(-\infty,-1)$, $-$ on $(-1,0)$, $+$ on $(0,1)$, $-$ on $(1,\infty)$. So maxima at $\pm1$, minimum at $0$.

**Answer: (D)**

iitjam-2024-26.title: General solution and discriminants
iitjam-2024-26.body:
The characteristic root is $1$ (double), and $x^2e^x$ is a particular solution (since $(x^2e^x)''-2(x^2e^x)'+x^2e^x=2e^x$). So
$$f(x)=(x^2+Bx+A)e^x,\qquad f'(x)=\big(x^2+(B+2)x+(A+B)\big)e^x.$$
- $f>0$ everywhere $\iff$ $\Delta_f=B^2-4A<0$.
- $f'>0$ everywhere $\iff$ $\Delta_{f'}=(B+2)^2-4(A+B)=B^2-4A+4<0$.

**Q true:** $\Delta_{f'}<0$ gives $B^2-4A<-4<0$.

**P false:** $A=\frac12$, $B=0$: $f=(x^2+\frac12)e^x>0$, but $\Delta_{f'}=-2+4=2>0$, so $f'=(x^2+2x+\frac12)e^x$ is negative near $x=-1$.

**Answer: (B)**

iitjam-2024-27.title: Sphere zone plus cylinder
iitjam-2024-27.body:
$D$ is a ball with a cylindrical hole. Let $h=\sqrt{a^2-b^2}$; the cylinder $x^2+y^2=b^2$ meets the sphere at $z=\pm h$.

- Outer boundary: the spherical zone $|z|\le h$. By Archimedes' hat-box theorem its area is $2\pi a\cdot2h=4\pi ah$.
- Inner boundary: the cylinder of radius $b$ and height $2h$: area $2\pi b\cdot2h=4\pi bh$.

Total: $4\pi(a+b)\sqrt{a^2-b^2}$.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-27.title: Integrate the zone area
iitjam-2024-27.body:
On the sphere, $dS=a\,dz\,d\theta$ (in cylindrical coordinates around the $z$-axis), so the zone $-h\le z\le h$ has area $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_{-h}^ha\,dz\,d\theta=4\pi ah$. Adding the cylinder $4\pi bh$ gives $4\pi(a+b)\sqrt{a^2-b^2}$.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-28.title: Take logarithms
iitjam-2024-28.body:
The apothem and circumradius satisfy $r_n=R_n\cos\frac\pi n$, so $\frac{R_n}{r_n}=\sec\frac\pi n$. Then
$$n^2\log\sec\frac\pi n=-n^2\log\cos\frac\pi n=-n^2\log\left(1-\frac{\pi^2}{2n^2}+O(n^{-4})\right)=\frac{\pi^2}{2}+O(n^{-2}).$$
So the limit is $e^{\pi^2/2}$.

**Answer: (B)**

iitjam-2024-28.title: Standard limit
iitjam-2024-28.body:
With $u=\pi/n\to0$: $n^2\log\sec u=\pi^2\cdot\frac{-\log\cos u}{u^2}$, and $\frac{-\log\cos u}{u^2}\to\frac12$ (L'Hôpital: $\frac{\tan u}{2u}\to\frac12$). So the exponent tends to $\frac{\pi^2}{2}$.

**Answer: (B)**

iitjam-2024-29.title: Rolle's theorem repeatedly
iitjam-2024-29.body:
Let $g(x)=f(x)-4x-3$, which has 4 distinct zeros. By Rolle, $g'$ has at least 3 zeros, $g''$ at least 2, $g'''$ at least 1. Since $g'''=f'''$, (C) holds.

The others are false:
- $h=f-3x-2$ has 3 zeros, so $h'=f'-3$ vanishes (at least twice): $f'$ attains 3. (A) false.
- $f''=g''$ has at least 2 zeros. (B) false.
- $f'$ attains 3 and 4, so by the intermediate value theorem ($f'$ is continuous) it attains $\frac72$. (D) false.

**Answer: (C)**

iitjam-2024-30.title: AM–GM in the positive quadrant
iitjam-2024-30.body:
For $x,y>0$ write $u=2x$, $v=3y$: $f=2uv\,e^{2-u-v}$. Since $te^{1-t}\le1$ with equality at $t=1$, we get $f=2(ue^{1-u})(ve^{1-v})\le2$, with equality at $u=v=1$, i.e. $(\frac12,\frac13)$. So the local maximum value is 2.

**Answer: (A)**

iitjam-2024-31.title: Check each statement
iitjam-2024-31.body:
**(A), (B) true.** If $\sum|a_n|$ converges then $a_n\to0$, so $|a_n|\le1$ for large $n$, and then $|a_n|^3\le|a_n|^2\le|a_n|$. Comparison gives absolute convergence.

**(C) false.** $a_n=\frac{(-1)^n}{\sqrt n}$: $\sum a_n$ converges (Leibniz) but $\sum a_n^2=\sum\frac1n$ diverges.

**(D) false.** Group terms in blocks of three: for $k=1,2,\dots$ use
$$\frac{1}{k^{1/3}},\ -\frac{1}{2k^{1/3}},\ -\frac{1}{2k^{1/3}}.$$
Each block sums to $0$ and the terms tend to $0$, so the partial sums tend to $0$: $\sum a_n$ converges. But the cubes in block $k$ sum to $\frac1k-\frac{2}{8k}=\frac{3}{4k}$, so $\sum a_n^3$ diverges.

**Answer: A, B**

iitjam-2024-32.title: Limit comparison
iitjam-2024-32.body:
Use $\log(1+u)\sim u$ and $1-\cos u\sim\frac{u^2}{2}$ as $u\to0$ (all terms are positive).

- (A) $n\log(1+n^{-3})\sim\frac1{n^2}$: convergent ✓.
- (B) $(1-\cos\frac1n)\log n\sim\frac{\log n}{2n^2}\le\frac{1}{2n^{3/2}}$ for large $n$: convergent ✓.
- (C) $n^2\log(1+n^{-3})\sim\frac1n$: divergent ✗.
- (D) $(1-\cos\frac1{\sqrt n})\log n\sim\frac{\log n}{2n}\ge\frac1{2n}$ for $n\ge3$: divergent ✗.

**Answer: A, B**

iitjam-2024-33.title: Isomorphism invariants
iitjam-2024-33.body:
- (A) True: $x\mapsto e^x$ is an isomorphism $(\mathbb R,+)\to(\mathbb R_{>0},\cdot)$ with inverse $\log$.
- (B) False: in $\mathbb R^*$ the only elements of finite order are $\pm1$, but $\mathbb C^*$ has $i$ of order 4.
- (C) False: $(\mathbb R,+)$ has no non-identity element of finite order, while $\mathbb C^*$ has $-1$ of order 2.
- (D) False: $\mathbb R$ is uncountable and $\mathbb Q$ is countable, so there is no bijection.

**Answer: A**

iitjam-2024-34.title: Primes versus even numbers
iitjam-2024-34.body:
- $f(2k)=2$ for every $k\ge1$, while $f(p)=p$ for every prime $p$. So $f$ takes the value 2 at arbitrarily large points and is unbounded: the limit does not exist (finite or infinite). (B) true, (A) false.
- For every prime $p>2024$, $p-1$ is even, so $f(p-1)=2<2024<p=f(p)$. By the intermediate value theorem there is $x\in(p-1,p)$ with $f(x)=2024$. These intervals are disjoint for different primes, and there are infinitely many primes, so the solution set is infinite. (D) true, (C) false.

**Answer: B, D**

iitjam-2024-35.title: Separate the variables
iitjam-2024-35.body:
$f(x,y)=u(x)+v(y)$ with $u(x)=2x^2-\log x$, $v(y)=3y^2-\frac16\log y$.

$u'(x)=4x-\frac1x$ vanishes only at $x=\frac12$, $u''=4+\frac1{x^2}>0$; $v'(y)=6y-\frac1{6y}$ vanishes only at $y=\frac16$, $v''>0$. So the only critical point is $(\frac12,\frac16)$, the Hessian there is positive definite, and $f$ is strictly convex: a unique local (indeed global) minimum, and no local maximum. (B) true, (A) false.

Level sets: $u$ and $v$ are bounded below (by $m_u=u(\frac12)$, $m_v=v(\frac16)$) and $u(x)\to\infty$ as $x\to0^+$ or $x\to\infty$, similarly $v$. If $f(x,y)=c$ then $u(x)\le c-m_v$ and $v(y)\le c-m_u$, which confine $x$ and $y$ to compact subintervals of $(0,\infty)$. So every level set is bounded. (C) true, (D) false.

**Answer: B, C**

iitjam-2024-36.title: Check each statement
iitjam-2024-36.body:
- **(A) false.** The dihedral group $D_4$ of order 8 has $Z=\{e,r^2\}$, and $D_4/Z$ has order 4, hence is abelian, so its center has 4 elements.
- **(B) true.** Pick $g\ne e$; $n\mapsto g^n$ is a homomorphism $\mathbb Z\to G$ that is non-trivial.
- **(C) true.** Since $G$ is non-abelian, some $a\notin Z(G)$; the inner automorphism $x\mapsto axa^{-1}$ is an isomorphism $G\to G$, and it is not the identity because $a$ fails to commute with some $x$.
- **(D) false.** $D_4$ (or the quaternion group) has order $8=2^3$ and is non-abelian.

**Answer: B, C**

iitjam-2024-37.title: Rows and columns of a product
iitjam-2024-37.body:
- The $i$-th row of $A=BC$ is $\sum_kb_{ik}\,(\text{row }k\text{ of }C)$, so Rowspace$(A)\subseteq$ Rowspace$(C)$ (B ✓).
- The $j$-th column of $A$ is $B\cdot(\text{column }j\text{ of }C)$, a combination of the columns of $B$, so Colspace$(A)\subseteq$ Colspace$(B)$ (C ✓).

(A) and (D) can fail. Let $E_{ij}$ be the matrix unit with a 1 in position $(i,j)$.
- $B=E_{11}$, $C=E_{12}$: $A=E_{12}$, whose row space is spanned by $e_2^T$, not contained in Rowspace$(B)=\langle e_1^T\rangle$.
- $B=E_{21}$, $C=E_{11}$: $A=E_{21}$, whose column space is $\langle e_2\rangle$, not contained in Colspace$(C)=\langle e_1\rangle$.

**Answer: B, C**

iitjam-2024-38.title: Bessel functions interlace
iitjam-2024-38.body:
Differentiating term by term,
$$f'(x)=\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{(-1)^m2m\,x^{2m-1}}{2^{2m}(m!)^2}=-\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-1)^k x^{2k+1}}{2^{2k+1}k!(k+1)!}=-g(x),$$
and similarly $(xg(x))'=\sum\frac{(-1)^m(2m+2)x^{2m+1}}{2^{2m+1}(m+1)!m!}=xf(x)$. ($f=J_0$, $g=J_1$.)

- Between consecutive zeros $x_1<x_2$ of $f$, Rolle gives a zero of $f'=-g$. If $g$ had two zeros $a<b$ in $(x_1,x_2)$, then $xg(x)$ would vanish at $a,b$, and Rolle applied to $xg$ would give a zero of $xf$ (hence of $f$) in $(a,b)\subset(x_1,x_2)$ — impossible. So $g$ vanishes exactly once in $(x_1,x_2)$.
- Between consecutive positive zeros $x_3<x_4$ of $g$, $xg$ vanishes at both ends, so $xf$, hence $f$, vanishes somewhere in between. If $f$ vanished twice there, $g=-f'$ would vanish between those two zeros, contradicting the choice of $x_3,x_4$. So $f$ vanishes exactly once in $(x_3,x_4)$.

**Answer: B, D**

iitjam-2024-38.title: Numerical sanity check
iitjam-2024-38.body:
The first positive zeros are $f$: $2.405,\ 5.520,\ 8.654,\dots$ and $g$: $3.832,\ 7.016,\ 10.17,\dots$ — they alternate, exactly one zero of each function between consecutive zeros of the other.

**Answer: B, D**

iitjam-2024-39.title: Shift by 2
iitjam-2024-39.body:
$x_{n+1}=-x_n^2+4x_n-2=2-(x_n-2)^2$. With $u_n=x_n-2$: $u_{n+1}=-u_n^2$, so $|u_n|=|u_1|^{2^{n-1}}$.

- If $|u_1|<1$, i.e. $\alpha\in(1,3)$, then $u_n\to0$ and $x_n\to2$.
- If $|u_1|>1$, i.e. $\alpha\in(0,1)\cup(3,4)$, then $|u_n|\to\infty$: divergent.

So the sequence converges for every $\alpha\in(1,2)$ and every $\alpha\in(2,3)$, and for no $\alpha\in(0,1)\cup(3,4)$.

**Answer: B, C**

iitjam-2024-40.title: Density and freeness
iitjam-2024-40.body:
- **(D) true.** $\phi(m,n)=m+n\sqrt2$ is a surjective homomorphism $\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z\to G$; it is injective because $m+n\sqrt2=0$ with $n\ne0$ would make $\sqrt2$ rational.
- **(A) false.** If $G=\langle c\rangle$, then $1=pc$ and $\sqrt2=qc$ for integers $p,q$, making $\sqrt2=q/p$ rational.
- **(B) true.** $\varepsilon=\sqrt2-1\in G$ with $0<\varepsilon<1$, so $\varepsilon^k\in G$ (closed under multiplication) gives arbitrarily small positive elements $\delta$ of $G$; the multiples $k\delta\in G$ hit every interval of length $>\delta$.
- **(C) false.** $G$ is dense by (B) but $G\ne\mathbb R$ (it is countable), so it is not closed.

**Answer: B, D**

iitjam-2024-41.title: Area above a hyperbola
iitjam-2024-41.body:
For $0<c\le1$, the part of the unit square with $xy\ge c$ is $\{c\le x\le1,\ c/x\le y\le1\}$, with area
$$A(c)=\int_c^1\left(1-\frac cx\right)dx=1-c+c\log c.$$
The required area is $A(\frac14)-A(\frac12)$:
$$\left(\tfrac34+\tfrac14\log\tfrac14\right)-\left(\tfrac12+\tfrac12\log\tfrac12\right)=\tfrac14-\tfrac12\log2+\tfrac12\log2=\tfrac14.$$

**Answer: 0.25**

iitjam-2024-41.title: Integrate in $x$ directly
iitjam-2024-41.body:
For $x\in[\frac14,\frac12]$, $y$ runs from $\frac1{4x}$ to $1$; for $x\in[\frac12,1]$, from $\frac1{4x}$ to $\frac1{2x}$:
$$\int_{1/4}^{1/2}\left(1-\frac1{4x}\right)dx+\int_{1/2}^1\frac{dx}{4x}=\frac14-\frac{\log2}{4}+\frac{\log2}{4}=\frac14.$$

**Answer: 0.25**

iitjam-2024-42.title: Solve
iitjam-2024-42.body:
Characteristic roots: $r^2+2r+5=0\Rightarrow r=-1\pm2i$. A constant particular solution is $y_p=\frac15$. So
$$y=\tfrac15+e^{-x}(C_1\cos2x+C_2\sin2x),$$
and the homogeneous part decays to 0 whatever $C_1,C_2$ are (here $C_1=-\frac15$, $C_2=\frac25$). Hence $y\to\frac15$.

**Answer: 0.20**

iitjam-2024-43.title: Write the solution
iitjam-2024-43.body:
$2r^2-r-1=0$ gives $r=1,-\frac12$, so $y=Ae^x+Be^{-x/2}$ with $A+B=1$, $A-\frac B2=\alpha$, i.e.
$$A=\frac{1+2\alpha}{3},\qquad B=\frac{2-2\alpha}{3}.$$
$y'=Ae^x-\frac B2e^{-x/2}=0\iff Ae^{3x/2}=\frac B2$. Since $\alpha>0$, $A>0$, and $Ae^{3x/2}$ takes every positive value. So there is a critical point iff $B>0$, i.e. $\alpha<1$.

For $\alpha\ge1$ there is none (at $\alpha=1$, $y=e^x$). The smallest such $\alpha$ is $1$.

**Answer: 1**

iitjam-2024-44.title: Solve $Mx=e_1$
iitjam-2024-44.body:
The first column of $M^{-1}$ solves $Mx=e_1$. Gaussian elimination gives $x=\left(-\frac13,\frac12,0,\frac16\right)$; check: row 1: $0+\frac12+0+\frac12=1$; row 2: $-\frac13+0+0+\frac13=0$; row 3: $-\frac23+\frac12+0+\frac16=0$; row 4: $-1+1+0+0=0$ ✓. So $a_{4,1}=\frac16$.

**Answer: 0.17**

iitjam-2024-45.title: Even polynomials with one constraint
iitjam-2024-45.body:
Even polynomials of degree $\le12$ are spanned by $1,x^2,x^4,\dots,x^{12}$: dimension 7. The condition $f(2024)=0$ is the kernel of the linear functional $f\mapsto f(2024)$, which is nonzero on this space (it sends $1\mapsto1$). So $\dim V=7-1=6$.

Explicit basis: $x^{2k}-2024^{2k}$ for $k=1,\dots,6$.

**Answer: 6**

iitjam-2024-46.title: Agree on the image
iitjam-2024-46.body:
- If $f$ is constant $c$: $c=c^{2024}$, so $c=0$ or $c^{2023}=1$, i.e. $c=1$ (real). Two functions.
- If $f$ is non-constant, its image is an infinite set (an interval), and on it $f(t)=t^{2024}$. Two polynomials agreeing at infinitely many points are equal, so $f(x)=x^{2024}$, which indeed works: $f(f(x))=(x^{2024})^{2024}=f(x)^{2024}$.

So $S=\{0,\ 1,\ x^{2024}\}$ has 3 elements.

**Answer: 3**

iitjam-2024-47.title: Telescoping
iitjam-2024-47.body:
Add the $n$-th terms of both series:
$$b_nc_na_{n+1}-a_nb_nc_n+a_{n+1}b_{n+1}c_{n+1}-a_{n+1}b_nc_n=a_{n+1}b_{n+1}c_{n+1}-a_nb_nc_n.$$
(Each series converges on its own, because $a_{n+1}-a_n$ and $b_{n+1}c_{n+1}-b_nc_n$ decay geometrically, see below.) So the total is $\lim a_nb_nc_n-a_1b_1c_1$.

The sum $a_n+b_n+c_n=6$ is preserved, and the differences halve in a rotating way: $a_{n+1}-b_{n+1}=\frac{a_n-c_n}{2}$ etc., so the maximum difference halves each step and all three converge to the common limit $L=6/3=2$.

Total $=2^3-1\cdot2\cdot3=8-6=2$.

**Answer: 2.00**

iitjam-2024-48.title: Polar coordinates (Viviani's problem)
iitjam-2024-48.body:
On the upper hemisphere $z=\sqrt{4-r^2}$, the area element is $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{4-r^2}}\,r\,dr\,d\theta$. The disc $(x-1)^2+y^2\le1$ is $r\le2\cos\theta$, $-\frac\pi2\le\theta\le\frac\pi2$. So
$$\text{Area}=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\int_0^{2\cos\theta}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-r^2}}\,dr\,d\theta=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}2\big(2-2|\sin\theta|\big)d\theta=4\pi-8.$$
$4\pi-8=4(\pi-2)\approx4.57$.

**Answer: 4.57**

iitjam-2024-48.title: Spherical coordinates
iitjam-2024-48.body:
On the sphere of radius 2, $x=2\sin\phi\cos\theta$, $y=2\sin\phi\sin\theta$; the condition $x^2+y^2\le2x$ becomes $\sin\phi\le\cos\theta$, i.e. $\phi\le\frac\pi2-|\theta|$ for $|\theta|\le\frac\pi2$ (upper hemisphere). With $dS=4\sin\phi\,d\phi\,d\theta$:
$$\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}4\big(1-\cos(\tfrac\pi2-|\theta|)\big)d\theta=4\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}(1-|\sin\theta|)d\theta=4(\pi-2).$$

**Answer: 4.57**

iitjam-2024-49.title: Stirling numbers of the second kind
iitjam-2024-49.body:
The coefficients of $x^n$ in the falling-factorial basis are the Stirling numbers $S(n,k)$: $x^n=\sum_kS(n,k)\,x(x-1)\cdots(x-k+1)$, where $S(n,k)$ counts partitions of an $n$-set into $k$ nonempty blocks. So $\alpha_{5,2}=S(5,2)$. A partition of $\{1,\dots,5\}$ into 2 blocks is an unordered pair $\{X,X^c\}$ with $X$ nonempty and proper: $\frac{2^5-2}{2}=15$.

**Answer: 15.00**

iitjam-2024-50.title: Companion-type matrix
iitjam-2024-50.body:
Take $p(x)=\det(xI-M)$ (the usual monic convention). $M$ has 2's on the subdiagonal and last column $(c_1,\dots,c_5)=(-1,-4,0,3,2)$; such a matrix is similar (via $\operatorname{diag}(1,2,4,8,16)$) to a companion matrix, and
$$p(x)=x^5-c_5x^4-2c_4x^3-4c_3x^2-8c_2x-16c_1=x^5-2x^4-6x^3+32x+16.$$
$p(2)=32-32-48+64+16=32$, so $p(2)-1=31$.

**Answer: 31**

iitjam-2024-50.title: Direct determinant at $x=2$
iitjam-2024-50.body:
$p(2)=\det(2I-M)=\det\begin{pmatrix}2&0&0&0&1\\-2&2&0&0&4\\0&-2&2&0&0\\0&0&-2&2&-3\\0&0&0&-2&0\end{pmatrix}$.
Expand along the first row: $p(2)=2\det A_{11}+(+1)\det A_{15}$, where
- $A_{15}$ (delete row 1, column 5) is upper triangular with diagonal $-2,-2,-2,-2$: $\det A_{15}=16$;
- $A_{11}=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&0&4\\-2&2&0&0\\0&-2&2&-3\\0&0&-2&0\end{pmatrix}$; expanding along its last row, $\det A_{11}=(-2)(-1)^{4+3}\det\begin{pmatrix}2&0&4\\-2&2&0\\0&-2&-3\end{pmatrix}=2\cdot(-12+16)=8$.

So $p(2)=16+16=32$ and $p(2)-1=31$.

(With the other convention $\det(M-xI)=-p(x)$ one would get $-33$; the standard monic characteristic polynomial gives 31.)

**Answer: 31**

iitjam-2024-51.title: Indicial equation
iitjam-2024-51.body:
Trying $y=x^r$: $r(r-1)+\alpha r+1=0$, i.e. $r^2+(\alpha-1)r+1=0$. The roots have product $1$ and sum $1-\alpha>1$.

- Real distinct roots: both positive (positive product and sum). Solutions $c_1x^{r_1}+c_2x^{r_2}\to0$.
- Double root $r=\frac{1-\alpha}{2}>0$: solutions $x^r(c_1+c_2\log x)\to0$.
- Complex roots $\mu\pm i\nu$ with $\mu=\frac{1-\alpha}2>0$: solutions $x^\mu(c_1\cos(\nu\log x)+c_2\sin(\nu\log x))\to0$.

So every $\alpha\in(-2\pi,0)$ is in $D$. The integers in $(-2\pi,0)\approx(-6.28,0)$ are $-6,\dots,-1$: six of them.

**Answer: 6**

iitjam-2024-52.title: Average of $\sin^2$
iitjam-2024-52.body:
$\sin^25x=\frac12-\frac12\cos10x$, so
$$\int_1^{\pi t}\frac{\sin^25x}{x}dx=\frac12\log(\pi t)-\frac12\int_1^{\pi t}\frac{\cos10x}{x}dx.$$
The last integral converges as $t\to\infty$ (Dirichlet test / integrate by parts), so it is bounded. Hence the integral is $\frac12\log t+O(1)$.

The prefactor: $\log(t^2+t^{-2})=2\log t+\log(1+t^{-4})=2\log t+o(1)$.

Ratio $\to\frac{1/2}{2}=\frac14=0.25$.

**Answer: 0.25**

iitjam-2024-52.title: Period by period
iitjam-2024-52.body:
$\sin^25x$ has period $\frac\pi5$ and mean $\frac12$. On $[k\frac\pi5,(k+1)\frac\pi5]$ the integral of $\frac{\sin^25x}{x}$ lies between $\frac{\pi/10}{(k+1)\pi/5}$ and $\frac{\pi/10}{k\pi/5}$, i.e. between $\frac{1}{2(k+1)}$ and $\frac{1}{2k}$. Summing $k$ up to about $5t$ gives $\frac12\log(5t)+O(1)=\frac12\log t+O(1)$, and dividing by $\log(t^2+t^{-2})\sim2\log t$ gives $\frac14$.

**Answer: 0.25**

iitjam-2024-53.title: Rotate the square
iitjam-2024-53.body:
Put $u=x-y$, $v=x+y$. Then $T$ becomes $[-1,1]\times[-1,1]$ and $dx\,dy=\frac12du\,dv$:
$$\frac12\int_{-1}^1\int_{-1}^1(\cos\pi u-\cos\pi v)^2\,du\,dv.$$
Using $\int_{-1}^1\cos^2\pi u\,du=1$ and $\int_{-1}^1\cos\pi u\,du=0$:
$$\frac12\big(2\cdot1+2\cdot1-2\cdot0\big)=2.$$

**Answer: 2.00**

iitjam-2024-53.title: Product form
iitjam-2024-53.body:
$\cos\pi(x-y)-\cos\pi(x+y)=2\sin\pi x\sin\pi y$, so the integral is $4\iint_T\sin^2\pi x\sin^2\pi y\,dx\,dy$. By symmetry this is $16$ times the integral over the first-quadrant triangle $x,y\ge0$, $x+y\le1$. Writing $\sin^2\theta=\frac{1-\cos2\theta}{2}$ and integrating over the triangle gives $\frac18$ for that piece, so the total is $16\cdot\frac18=2$ (a numerical integration confirms $2.000$).

**Answer: 2.00**

iitjam-2024-54.title: Symmetry of the ball
iitjam-2024-54.body:
By symmetry, $\iiint_Sxy=\iiint_Syz=\iiint_Szx=0$ and $\iiint_Sx^2=\iiint_Sy^2=\iiint_Sz^2=\frac13\iiint_S\rho^2\,dV=\frac13\int_0^14\pi\rho^4d\rho=\frac{4\pi}{15}$.

So only the squared coefficients matter. Coefficient of $x^2$: $1+4+1=6$; of $y^2$: $4+1+1=6$; of $z^2$: $1+1+4=6$. The integral is $18\cdot\frac{4\pi}{15}=\frac{24\pi}{5}$, and dividing by $\pi$ gives $\frac{24}{5}=4.8$.

**Answer: 4.80**

iitjam-2024-55.title: Squeeze
iitjam-2024-55.body:
For $1\le k\le n$: $\frac{k^2}{n^3+n}\le\frac{k^2}{n^3+k}\le\frac{k^2}{n^3}$. Summing with $\sum k^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$:
$$\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6(n^3+n)}\le a_n\le\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6n^3}.$$
Both bounds tend to $\frac26=\frac13$. So $a_n\to\frac13\approx0.33$.

**Answer: 0.33**

iitjam-2024-55.title: Riemann sum
iitjam-2024-55.body:
$a_n=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{(k/n)^2}{1+k/n^3}\cdot\frac1n$, and $1\le1+k/n^3\le1+1/n^2$, so $a_n$ has the same limit as $\frac1n\sum(k/n)^2\to\int_0^1t^2dt=\frac13$.

**Answer: 0.33**

iitjam-2024-56.title: Local extrema
iitjam-2024-56.body:
$f'(x)=3x^2-8x+4=(3x-2)(x-2)$. Local max at $x=\frac23$: $f(\frac23)=\frac8{27}-\frac{16}9+\frac83-6=-\frac{130}{27}\approx-4.81$. Local min at $x=2$: $f(2)=-6$.

A cubic with positive leading coefficient takes a value $c$ three times iff $-6<c<-\frac{130}{27}$, and once if $c<-6$ or $c>-\frac{130}{27}$.

- $c=-7<-6$: 1 solution.
- $c=-5\in(-6,-4.81)$: 3 solutions.
- $c=3>-4.81$: 1 solution.

Total $1+3+1=5$.

**Answer: 5**

iitjam-2024-56.title: Note $f(x)=x(x-2)^2-6$
iitjam-2024-56.body:
$f(x)+6=x(x-2)^2$. So $f(x)=c$ means $x(x-2)^2=c+6$.

- $c+6=-1$: $x(x-2)^2<0$ needs $x<0$, where $x(x-2)^2$ is increasing from $-\infty$ to $0$: one solution.
- $c+6=1$: $g(x)=x(x-2)^2$ rises from 0 to $g(\frac23)=\frac{32}{27}>1$, falls to $g(2)=0$, then rises: three solutions.
- $c+6=9>\frac{32}{27}$: one solution (with $x>2$).

**Answer: 5**

iitjam-2024-57.title: Symmetry
iitjam-2024-57.body:
The integral is over the triangle $0\le x\le y\le c$. The integrand $e^{x^2+y^2}$ is symmetric in $x,y$, so the integral over the triangle is half of the integral over the square $[0,c]^2$:
$$\frac12\left(\int_0^ce^{x^2}dx\right)\left(\int_0^ce^{y^2}dy\right)=\frac12\cdot3\cdot3=4.5.$$

**Answer: 4.5**

iitjam-2024-57.title: Antiderivative trick
iitjam-2024-57.body:
Let $F(t)=\int_0^te^{s^2}ds$. The inner integral is $e^{x^2}(F(c)-F(x))$, so the double integral is
$$\int_0^cF'(x)(F(c)-F(x))\,dx=\Big[F(c)F(x)-\tfrac12F(x)^2\Big]_0^c=\tfrac12F(c)^2=\tfrac92.$$

**Answer: 4.5**

iitjam-2024-58.title: Values at the nodes
iitjam-2024-58.body:
A continuous piecewise linear function on $[0,1]$ with nodes $\frac14,\frac12,\frac34$ is determined by its values at $0,\frac14,\frac12,\frac34,1$ (linear interpolation on each of the 4 pieces), and any 5 values give such a function. So $f\mapsto\big(f(0),f(\frac14),f(\frac12),f(\frac34),f(1)\big)$ is an isomorphism $V\to\mathbb R^5$.

**Answer: 5**

iitjam-2024-58.title: Count parameters
iitjam-2024-58.body:
Four pieces give $8$ parameters $(a_j,b_j)$; continuity at the three interior nodes imposes 3 independent linear conditions. $8-3=5$. A basis: $1,\ t,\ (t-\frac14)_+,\ (t-\frac12)_+,\ (t-\frac34)_+$.

**Answer: 5**

iitjam-2024-59.title: Integrate the binomial theorem
iitjam-2024-59.body:
$\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk\frac{n^k}{k+1}=\frac1n\int_0^n(1+t)^n\,dt=\frac{(1+n)^{n+1}-1}{n(n+1)}$, since $\int_0^n\binom nkt^kdt=\binom nk\frac{n^{k+1}}{k+1}$.

So
$$a_n=\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}-1}{n^n(n+1)}=\left(1+\frac1n\right)^n-\frac{1}{n^n(n+1)}\to e.$$
Hence $\beta=e$ and $\log\beta=1$.

**Answer: 1.00**

iitjam-2024-59.title: Use $\frac{1}{k+1}\binom nk=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{n+1}{k+1}$
iitjam-2024-59.body:
$\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{n+1}{k+1}n^k=\frac{1}{n(n+1)}\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}\binom{n+1}{j}n^j=\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}-1}{n(n+1)}$, the same expression, so $a_n\to e$ and $\log\beta=1$.

**Answer: 1.00**

iitjam-2024-60.title: A differential equation for $y=(\sin^{-1}x)^2$
iitjam-2024-60.body:
$y'=\frac{2\sin^{-1}x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$, so $(1-x^2)y'^2=4y$. Differentiating and dividing by $2y'$: $(1-x^2)y''-xy'=2$.

With $y=\sum a_nx^n$ ($a_0=a_1=0$), comparing coefficients of $x^n$: $(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2}-n(n-1)a_n-na_n=2\delta_{n0}$, i.e.
$$a_{n+2}=\frac{n^2}{(n+1)(n+2)}a_n\ (n\ge1),\qquad a_2=1.$$
So $a_4=\frac{4}{12}=\frac13$, $a_6=\frac{16}{30}\cdot\frac13=\frac{8}{45}$, and $9a_6=\frac85=1.6$.

**Answer: 1.60**

iitjam-2024-60.title: Square the arcsine series
iitjam-2024-60.body:
$\sin^{-1}x=x+\frac{x^3}{6}+\frac{3x^5}{40}+\cdots$. The $x^6$ coefficient of the square is $2\cdot\frac{3}{40}+\left(\frac16\right)^2=\frac{3}{20}+\frac1{36}=\frac{27+5}{180}=\frac{8}{45}$. So $9a_6=\frac85$.

**Answer: 1.60**
